chapter: Swing, singers, Ed Fox and recordings
title: Repeating the same solo versus improvising
summary: Common to repeat solos; some never played the same twice.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Speaking of choruses, there seems to be some of the older musicians -- well, do you know Jimmy Granada?
Jimmy's a beautiful player, beautiful man.

But he plays the same solo on whatever the tune is, everytime it's played. And a lot of guys used to do that. Barney Bigard used to do that, you know, one -- if they were going to play "Tiger Rag" then he always played this solo. If they were going to play whatever it was, "A Closer Walk With Thee," you'd always hear the same solo, sort of worked the same melody, beautiful solos.
Was that pretty common back in the twenties, or did most of the guys do as we do now, you know, just try to play something different each time?
No, that was pretty common back in those days. But there was some artists that never played the same thing twice. Well, that was their talent.
The ear. Just get up and blow. And listen to the chord structure, and try to keep the melody in mind, but play around the melody.
Right. Jimmy Noone was sort of like that, I understand.
Always wanted the melody going on behind him when he soloed?
That's interesting, those two approaches to the solo.
